A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting network learned to press DONE at once (0% success, 100% DONE before any placement). The cause is the hidden rule. The target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, with wrap-around. The starting network only sees about 2 cells either side of a cell (1x1 stem plus two 3x3 convs), so it can never see the target cells for the column it is building in. With no usable signal, every placement has negative expected reward, and DONE (reward 0) wins. The first fix is perception: each cell needs learned access to features 4 columns away, around the wrap. Two ways to give it this: (a) a full-width convolution along x with wrap-around padding, which can learn any column shift, and (b) attention with a learned position bias that wraps around in x. Recipe is a second question. The default recipe gives only about 32 PPO updates, so halving n_envs to double the updates is also tested.

### Round 2
The hidden 4-column wrap-around shift was the real problem. The start network has only local receptive fields, so it could not line up build and target, and it learned to press DONE at once. Any module that can reach across the wrap fixes this: the row conv scored 0.36, then 0.65 with twice as many updates, and the attention with wrap-around bias scored 0.81. Halving n_envs raised success by about 0.29. That is bigger than the seed spread seen so far (up to 0.24 between seeds), so the number of updates matters. Every learning curve was still rising at the end, and training took only 57–75 s of the 900 s limit. So the runs are short of updates or samples, not compute time. Attention beat the row conv by 0.16 with the same recipe, which is about the size of the seed noise. Mean IoU near 0.97 suggests that the failures are small ordering or overhang mistakes, not misalignment. Plan: two recipe refinements of the best network, and one test of a second, later attention layer for global context.

### Round 3
The main way trials fail is collapse into pressing DONE at once. Early random placements earn negative reward and DONE earns 0, so each run is a race: learn the 4-column shift before settling on DONE. The 2-epoch run collapsed on both seeds. With n_envs 64, one seed scored 0.87 and the other collapsed to 0. Even the best run (r1c3, 0.81) fell to a mean episode length of 2.8 before recovering. Wrap-around attention lines up the target best (0.81 vs 0.65 for the row convolution), and more, smaller updates helped (n_envs 128 beat 256: 0.65 vs 0.36). A second attention block after the trunk slowed learning (0.125). Next: (1) a higher entropy bonus to stop the DONE collapse; (2) the same change with n_envs 64; (3) separate stems for build and shifted target, with cross-attention so the target can be lined up before any local mixing.

### Round 4
Aligning the shifted target is the key: none of 0, wrap-around row conv 0.65, wrap-around attention 0.81. Most of the gap between runs is seed collapse into early DONE, not skill. r2c1 scored 0.87 on one seed and 0 on the other; both seeds of r2c2 collapsed, as did one seed of r3c2. Runs that survive score about 0.75–0.88. Entropy 0.02 did not stop collapse. A second attention block and split stems both slowed learning. Collapse happens because random placements cost reward until the shift is learned. So the most promising levers are (a) learning the alignment faster: attention values taken by a linear map straight from the raw observation, so the shifted target arrives intact, and (b) a standard near-uniform policy start (small output-layer init), so DONE gets no early lead. Last round: test each lever alone on r1c3, plus both together.

## Trial it ended with
name: attention with wrap-around bias
hypothesis: Inserts one multi-head self-attention layer over all cells after the stem, before the 3x3 trunk. Each head has a learned position bias indexed by row offset and by column offset with wrap-around; the bias starts at zero and is scaled up so it can learn quickly. Heads can learn to attend 3, 4 or 5 columns over, bringing in target features. The recipe matches the second candidate. If it scores clearly below the second candidate, attention learns the shift too slowly for this budget.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).
